html:
A rice market at Dōjima in Osaka, Japan, where merchants traded rice and rice futures from 1697. It is often called the first organised futures exchange in the world.

In Tokugawa Japan lords drew their income as rice taxes and needed cash. They shipped rice to warehouses in Osaka and sold receipts for it. Traders at Dōjima bought and sold these rice tickets, and from them grew contracts for rice to be delivered later. Prices were set by open bidding, and contracts were standard and settled through clearing houses, much like modern futures.

The shogunate at first distrusted this trade as gambling, then came to recognise it, and in 1773 took it under official sponsorship. Rice prices set at Dōjima were sent across Japan by flag signals and runners. The trader Homma Munehisa, according to tradition, invented the candlestick charts still used by traders around the world.

The exchange lasted until 1939, when wartime controls folded it into a state rice agency.
